questions.question: Abstract class vs Interface in Java 8+ — fields, constructors, default/static methods, multiple inheritance: when do you reach for each?
questions.title: Abstract Class vs Interface in Java 8+ — Complete Comparison with Decision Rules
questions.direct_answer: **Abstract class** = partial implementation + state. Supports **instance fields**, **constructors**, **protected/package-private members**, single inheritance only (`extends`). **Interface** = pure contract, with `default` and `static` methods since Java 8 and `private` helpers since Java 9. Supports **public constants only** (no instance state), **no constructors**, a class can implement **many** interfaces. **Decision rule:** use an interface to declare a **capability** (`Comparable`, `Flyable`, `Serializable`); use an abstract class when you have **shared state or protected infrastructure** for a family of related types (e.g., `AbstractList`, `HttpServlet`).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the post-Java 8 landscape — default and static methods narrowed the gap — and still knows the remaining differences: state, constructors, access modifiers, inheritance count
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming interfaces can't have method bodies (pre-Java 8 thinking). Forgetting that interfaces have no instance state. Not knowing about private interface methods (Java 9)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the decision framework — capability vs family — and explain why JDK uses both (List interface + AbstractList skeletal implementation). Mention that Java 14+ sealed interfaces change the picture again

sections.title: The Line Between Them Moved in Java 8 — Here's Where It Sits Now
sections.content:
Before Java 8, the distinction was simple: abstract classes had method bodies, interfaces didn't. Java 8 blurred that by adding `default` and `static` methods to interfaces, and Java 9 added `private` interface methods. After those changes the question became: what's actually different anymore?

The answer is still two things: **state** and **inheritance model**. An abstract class can hold instance fields and define a constructor to initialize them; subclasses inherit that state. An interface cannot — its only fields are implicit `public static final` constants. A class can `extends` **exactly one** abstract class but `implements` **many** interfaces.

That's why the JDK itself uses both: `List` is an interface (the capability contract — any collection that acts like a list), and `AbstractList` is an abstract class (the shared skeletal implementation with `modCount`, iterator machinery, etc.). Concrete classes like `ArrayList` extend `AbstractList` for state and implement `List` for the contract.

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface (Java 17+)
Every Difference That Still Matters After Java 8+
sections.content:
| Feature | Abstract Class | Interface (Java 8+) |
|---|---|---|
| Instance fields | Yes | No (only `public static final` constants) |
| Constructors | Yes (called by subclasses via `super()`) | No |
| Method bodies | Abstract + concrete | Abstract + `default` + `static` + `private` (Java 9+) |
| Access modifiers on members | `public`, `protected`, package-private, `private` | Methods are implicitly `public` (private allowed Java 9+) |
| Inheritance | Single (`extends`) | Multiple (`implements A, B, C`) |
| `final` methods | Allowed | Not allowed — all methods are implicitly overridable |
| `static` methods | Yes | Yes (Java 8+) |
| Can hold mutable state | Yes | No |
| Constructor can run setup logic | Yes | No — use a `default` factory method or the implementing class's constructor |
| Used for | Shared infrastructure for related types | Declaring a capability applicable to unrelated types |
| JDK examples | `AbstractList`, `HttpServlet`, `InputStream` | `List`, `Comparable`, `Runnable`, `Serializable` |

sections.title: When Abstract Class Fits — Shared State and Protected Infrastructure
When Interface Fits — Capability Across Unrelated Types
The Decision Framework — Capability vs Family
sections.content:
Use this mental model when you're deciding between them.

**Use an interface when:**
- You're expressing a **capability** that can apply to unrelated types (`Comparable`, `Serializable`, `AutoCloseable`).
- You need multiple inheritance — a class needs to expose more than one contract.
- You want the JDK-style decoupled design — many unrelated implementations of the same contract.
- Java 14+: you want a **sealed** interface to restrict implementors (`sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle`).

**Use an abstract class when:**
- You have **shared state** (fields) across a family of related types.
- You need **constructor logic** to validate or initialize that state.
- You want to lock down some methods with `final` while leaving others abstract or default.
- You want **protected** members accessible only to subclasses — interfaces can't express that.

**The JDK's own answer:** use both together. Declare the contract as an interface (`List`), provide a skeletal implementation as an abstract class (`AbstractList`), and let concrete classes extend the skeleton while implementing the contract. This gives implementors a choice: use the shortcut (extend) or start from scratch (just implement).

sections.title: Pragmatic Trade-offs in Real Code
sections.content:
**Interfaces + default methods for evolution, abstract classes for investment**
- Default methods let you add functionality to an interface **without breaking existing implementors** — that's how `Collection.stream()` and `forEach()` were added retroactively in Java 8.
- Abstract classes can't be evolved the same way — adding a new abstract method breaks every subclass. Adding a concrete method is safer but subclasses override semantics unexpectedly.

**Avoid deep abstract hierarchies**
- 4+ levels of abstract classes = fragile design; any change cascades through every level.
- Prefer composition + interfaces: `class User implements Serializable, Comparable<User>, Validator` is often cleaner than `extends AbstractUser extends AbstractPerson`.

**When to use both (the JDK pattern)**
- `interface Shape { double area(); }` + `abstract class AbstractShape implements Shape { ... shared fields ... }` + `class Circle extends AbstractShape`
- Gives you best of both — capability contract for decoupled code, skeletal implementation for convenience.

**Sealed interfaces (Java 17+)**
- Restrict which types can implement — `sealed interface Event permits UserCreated, UserDeleted`.
- Enables exhaustive `switch` expressions.
- Narrow the abstract class niche further — now interfaces can express closed type hierarchies.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstract class = state + infrastructure**; interface = pure capability contract.
- **Single vs multiple inheritance** is the practical non-negotiable difference.
- **Interfaces have no instance fields or constructors** — only `public static final` constants.
- **Java 8+ interfaces have `default`, `static`, and (since 9) `private` methods** — but still no state.
- **JDK uses both** — `List` interface + `AbstractList` skeletal implementation pattern.
- **Default methods enable safe API evolution** — abstract classes can't be evolved as gracefully.
- **Sealed interfaces (Java 17+)** give interfaces closed-hierarchy semantics without the state trade-off.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
After Java 8, the line between them moved — interfaces got `default`, `static`, and (since Java 9) `private` methods, so the real differences come down to **state** and **inheritance**.

**What still only abstract classes can do**
- Hold instance fields and mutable state
- Define constructors that run initialization logic
- Use `protected` and package-private access on members
- Mark methods `final` to lock them down

**What only interfaces can do**
- Be implemented by many types from unrelated hierarchies (`implements A, B, C`)
- Be added to a type retroactively without disrupting its single-inheritance chain
- Evolve safely via `default` methods without breaking existing implementors

**The decision framework**
- Interface = **capability** that can apply to unrelated types (`Comparable`, `AutoCloseable`, `Flyable`)
- Abstract class = **family** of related types that share state and protected infrastructure (`AbstractList`, `HttpServlet`)
- The JDK pattern uses both together — `List` interface + `AbstractList` skeletal implementation

**Sealed interfaces (Java 17+)**
- Restrict which types implement an interface — `sealed interface Event permits UserCreated, UserDeleted`
- Enables exhaustive `switch` expressions; narrows the abstract class niche further

**Recommendation:** Default to **interfaces** for declaring contracts — they're more flexible and safer to evolve. Reach for an **abstract class** when multiple concrete types will share state or protected setup logic, and consider combining them (JDK pattern) when you want to offer both a clean contract and a convenience skeleton.

groups.heading: Abstract class
groups.text: Can mix in state. It holds instance fields, a constructor, protected helpers. Subclasses extend it — one only.

groups.heading: Interface
groups.text: Pure contract — no instance state. Single inheritance for classes, multiple for interfaces. Default methods since Java 8 narrowed the gap.

groups.heading: Abstract class
groups.text: Pick it when subclasses share state or lifecycle — like AbstractList carrying modCount.

groups.heading: Interface
groups.text: Pick it when unrelated types need the same contract — Comparable, Runnable, AutoCloseable. The gotcha: default methods let you evolve an interface without breaking existing implementors.
